title: Praise
hookLine: hands raised, songs repeated, worship loud and joyful

lines: THE ARK COMES UP TO JERUSALEM.
DAVID DANCES WITH ALL HIS MIGHT.
cards: The ark of God is coming up into Jerusalem, with shouting and the sound of the trumpet, and the king can't keep still. "And David danced before the LORD with all his might."
His wife Michal watches from a window and despises him for it. A king, leaping in the street. David's answer: he'll be lowlier still in his own eyes, before the LORD who chose him.
A new week opens with Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, whose worship can look a lot like David in the street.

teach.b: Step into a Pentecostal or charismatic service and you may find a band, a congregation on its feet, hands in the air, one chorus sung again and again, someone calling out amen, someone in tears, someone very still.
From the back row it can look like a concert. To the people there, it's praise: thanking God out loud, with the whole body. Much of it has old roots.
Psalm 134 says, "Lift up your hands in the sanctuary, and bless the LORD." Paul's first letter to Timothy pictures people praying everywhere, "lifting up holy hands."
Open hands, held up, the way a child reaches for a parent. The repeated songs have old roots too.

teach.h: FOR HIS MERCY ENDURETH FOR EVER.
teach.b: Psalm 136 gives reason after reason to thank God, and every verse ends with the same answer: "for his mercy endureth for ever." Again and again, until the line isn't something you think about but something you stand on.
Hallelujah comes from the psalms as well.
Psalm 150 ends, in the King James, "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD." That last phrase, in Hebrew, is hallelujah.
Christians praise at very different volumes: Orthodox chant, a quiet Anglican evensong, the silence of a Quaker meeting, a Pentecostal church on its feet. The psalms make room for all of them.

teach.h: BE STILL, OR CLAP YOUR HANDS.
teach.b: The same book that says "Be still, and know that I am God" also says, "O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph."

how: In Pentecostal and charismatic churches, worship often includes a band, raised hands, repeated choruses and spoken praise; other churches praise through chant, hymns or silence.

o: a style of loud church music with a band
thanking God out loud, with songs and the whole body
flattering God so that prayers will be answered

p: danced before the LORD with all his might
lift up your hands in the sanctuary
for his mercy endureth for ever

s: lifting hands in worship is a modern invention
Psalm 134: "Lift up your hands in the sanctuary"; 1 Timothy: "lifting up holy hands."
Psalm 136 ends every verse with the same words
"for his mercy endureth for ever," again and again.
the psalms only make room for quiet worship
the same book says "be still" and "O clap your hands, all ye people."

games.q: you're David. you've danced before the LORD in the street, and your wife says it was beneath a king. what do you say?
o: she's right; it won't happen again.
I'll be lowlier still, before the LORD who chose me.
games.why: David doesn't apologize. he says he'll be even lowlier in his own eyes, because the dancing was before the LORD.

practice: If you're somewhere you can, lift your hands, palms open, to shoulder height or higher, and hold them there for a few slow breaths; it may feel unusual, and that's all right. Then lower them slowly to your lap, and rest.
If you pray, say the psalms' last line, Praise ye the LORD; if you don't, let your open hands be a thank-you for one good thing today.

wordCard.voice: Praise. Thanking God out loud, with songs, raised hands and the whole body. In Hebrew, hallelujah.

orig.note: Hebrew: hallelujah. at the end of Psalm 150 the King James renders it praise ye the LORD.

carryVoice: Your line: hands up. Open hands, the way a child reaches. I'll be here tomorrow.
